name: Missi powder (tooth/gum blackening)

card.summary: A traditional South Asian powder of iron and copper sulphate and tannin-rich myrobalans rubbed on the teeth and gums to darken them as a beauty and social custom.
card.note: Metal-salt ingredients; no modern clinical research.

quick.overview:
Missī (also spelled misi) was a powder used in parts of South Asia to blacken the gums and sometimes the teeth. It was made from iron and copper sulphate, a tannin-rich plant source such as myrobalans, and flavouring agents.[1]

The appearance payoff was cultural: dark gums and teeth were a mark of adult beauty and status in the settings where it was used, and it is described as having been bound up with courtesan culture, where it was tied to a ritual.[1] Medicinal benefit is described as a minor motive.[1]
quick.how: It was applied as a powder to the gums and teeth as a cosmetic routine, mainly by women in some Hindu communities. Related traditions elsewhere used plant tars or chewed plant products instead.[1]
quick.risks: No modern clinical studies of missi were identified. Because it contains metal sulphates, it is a subject of dental and toxicology interest, but this page does not rely on trial data. The custom has largely declined since colonial-era Western beauty standards spread.[1]

lead: Missī is a South Asian cosmetic powder used to darken the gums and sometimes the teeth. According to Wikipedia's article on tooth blackening, it combined iron and copper sulphate, a tannin-rich plant source such as myrobalans, and flavourings.[1]

Dark teeth and gums were an aesthetic ideal in many Southeast Asian and Oceanic cultures, in pre-Meiji Japan and in parts of India. Colonial-era Western beauty standards contributed to the decline of the practice.[1] In courtesan culture missī became associated with a ritual; some Hindu practitioners used it mainly for the gums; medicinal benefits were a minor motivation.[1] The chemistry is comparable to Japanese ohaguro, which used iron acetate with plant tannins in the manner of iron gall ink.[2]

chain: Iron/copper salts react with tannins from myrobalans
Look matching the beauty norms of the tradition
angle.text: It changes the colour of the gums and teeth to black, a look that was the beauty standard in the communities where it was used. It is a traditional cosmetic rather than a whitening product.

infobox: Iron and copper sulphate, myrobalans, flavourings[1]

paras: The powder was made from iron and copper sulphate, a plant source of tannins such as myrobalans, and flavouring agents.[1] Some Hindu practitioners blackened mainly the gums, and sometimes the teeth.[1] Groups in the Eastern Himalayas used plant wood tar or chewed plant products instead.[1]

The Wikipedia article reports that in courtesan and prostitute culture missī became synonymous with a ritual associated with selling a woman's virginity.[1] Medicinal benefit was a minor motivation.[1] Related traditions elsewhere were tied to coming of age, marriage and social identity, as with Japanese ohaguro, which was banned for men in 1870 and faded after the Meiji period.[2]
